Rutland.wildlife_intro:
Rutland is a small city with a full urban wildlife list: raccoons and skunks throughout the neighborhoods, squirrels in the mature street trees, rats around older commercial blocks and alleys, and bats in the tall attics of its older homes. Pine Hill's woods sit inside the city, and Otter Creek's corridor moves animals through town nightly, so even quiet streets see regular visitors.

Fall brings the mouse and squirrel rush into older housing, spring brings denning raccoons in chimneys and skunks under porches, and summer bat colonies are exclusion only — one-way doors in spring and late August through fall, proofing from December through March, and no colony work while pups cannot fly. Our crew works Rutland street by street, and a whole-building inspection is standard, because city homes rarely have just one entry.

Fair Haven.wildlife_intro:
Fair Haven's older slate-era housing gives bats, squirrels, and raccoons plenty of ways in, and its river farms add skunks, woodchucks, and barn animals to the list. Opossums are established in the Champlain lowlands and turn up here under decks and in outbuildings. Western Rutland County is also Vermont's only timber rattlesnake country — the snake is endangered, found in the rocky ledges around West Haven, and any rattlesnake call is referral-only to Vermont Fish and Wildlife, never a removal job.

Our crew's Fair Haven year is fall proofing, spring denning calls, and summer bat exclusions timed for spring or late August through fall with one-way doors, with winter reserved for proofing empty attics. No bat colony work happens while pups are flightless. If you ever see a heavy-bodied snake with a rattle near the western ledges, keep your distance and call Vermont Fish and Wildlife — and call us for everything else in the house and barn.

faqs.q: What should I do if I see a rattlesnake near Fair Haven?
faqs.a: Leave it alone and keep people and pets back. The timber rattlesnake is endangered, is Vermont's only venomous snake, and in this state lives only in western Rutland County. It is referral-only: contact Vermont Fish and Wildlife rather than any removal company. Most snakes seen here are harmless racers, ratsnakes, or garters — those our crew can help identify.
